title: EV, implied odds, semi-bluffs
description: Six questions on multi-street decisions and the EV calculus that supports them.

questions.prompt: Pot is 100bb. You bluff 50bb on the river with zero equity if called. Villain folds 30% of the time. What is the EV of the bluff (in bb)?
questions.explanation: EV = 0.30 · 100 + 0.70 · (-50) = 30 - 35 = -5bb. α here is 50/150 ≈ 33.3%, so a 30% fold rate falls short and the bluff loses on average.

questions.prompt: Pot is 10bb, you bet 7bb with a flush draw. Villain folds 35% and when called you have 35% equity. What is the approximate EV (in bb, 1 decimal)?
questions.explanation: Fold leg: 0.35 · 10 = 3.5. Call leg: 0.65 · (0.35 · 17 - 0.65 · 7) = 0.65 · 1.4 = 0.91. Total ≈ 4.4bb. Semi-bluffs combine fold and showdown EV.

questions.prompt: Why is a semi-bluff often profitable when villain folds far less than α?

choices.text: Because fold equity does not factor into a semi-bluff's EV.
Because showdown equity provides a second source of EV that compounds with whatever folds you do generate.
Because villain is forced to call any draw.
Because semi-bluffs do not risk chips when called.

questions.explanation: α is derived for *zero-equity* bluffs. With showdown equity in the mix, the call leg also produces positive EV, lowering the fold rate required to break even.

questions.prompt: Turn: pot 50bb, villain bets 50bb. You have a draw with 18% equity. What is the break-even additional X (in bb, integer)?
questions.explanation: X = (C - eq · (P + C)) / eq = (50 - 0.18·100) / 0.18 = 32 / 0.18 ≈ 178bb. With 100bb stacks behind, this is unrealistic — the call is bad.

questions.prompt: When chasing a non-nut flush draw against a tight player, you should still apply your full implied odds — the formula doesn't care which suit you hold.
questions.explanation: Non-nut draws are the textbook reverse-implied-odds spot: when you hit and bet, villain often holds the higher draw and raises; when you miss, you lose minimally. Discount implied odds heavily — sometimes to zero or negative.

questions.prompt: Which scenario has the LEAST useful implied odds?

choices.text: 100bb effective, opponent bets 50% pot on the turn — pot 50, bet 25.
All-in on the turn — no chips remain behind.
Deep-stacked (250bb), opponent bets pot on the flop.
200bb stacks against a calling station who never folds postflop.

questions.explanation: Implied odds depend on winning *future* money. When the bet is all-in, there is no future money to be won and the X term collapses to zero — only naked pot odds apply.
